chapters.title: Chapter 3: Hidden Markov Models for Regime Identification

lessons.title: Hidden Markov Models Explained: States You Can't See, Data You Can

body.text: A Hidden Markov Model is two coupled stories running at once: a hidden regime that quietly switches according to its own rules, and an observed return series that reveals just enough about that hidden regime to let you infer it.

children.text: Chapter 2 ended with a toy Bayesian update: a prior belief, one observation, a posterior belief. A Hidden Markov Model, HMM from here on, is what you get when you formalize that idea properly, repeat it every day, and let a learned transition structure replace the fixed prior. This lesson defines an HMM precisely, before the next three lessons show you how to fit one on real Nifty data.
The Generative Story: How an HMM 'Makes' a Return Series

The clearest way to understand an HMM is to imagine the process that supposedly generated your data, even though nobody actually generates markets this way. It is a useful fiction that makes every piece of the model concrete.

body.caption: The generative story behind a Hidden Markov Model

cells: Choose the initial hidden state, z₁, from an initial distribution π
Draw today's return, x₁, from the emission distribution attached to state z₁
Choose tomorrow's state, z₂, using the transition matrix row for z₁
Draw tomorrow's return, x₂, from the emission distribution attached to state z₂
Repeat: each new state depends only on the previous state, and each new return depends only on the current state

children.text: Step 5 hides two strong assumptions that are worth stating precisely, because everything else in this chapter depends on them.

body.latex: P(z_t \mid z_{t-1}, z_{t-2}, \ldots, z_1) = P(z_t \mid z_{t-1})
body.caption: The Markov property: tomorrow's hidden state depends only on today's state, not on the full history

body.latex: P(x_t \mid z_t, x_{t-1}, z_{t-1}, \ldots) = P(x_t \mid z_t)
body.caption: Conditional independence of observations: today's return depends only on today's hidden state

body.text: Neither assumption is literally true of real markets. Momentum and volatility clustering both suggest real dependence beyond just yesterday. The Markov property is a deliberate simplification that makes estimation tractable, not a claim that markets are literally memoryless. Whether the simplification costs you more than it saves is exactly the kind of question Chapter 7's backtesting discipline is built to answer.

children.text: Two States, One Nifty Return Series

Here is a concrete, illustrative two-state HMM for Nifty daily returns: a calm state and a stressed state. Each state carries its own emission distribution, modeled here as a normal distribution of daily returns, and its own self-transition probability, the diagonal entry of the transition matrix that determines how persistent the state is.

body.caption: An illustrative 2-state HMM for Nifty daily returns

body.text: These parameters are illustrative, chosen by hand to be plausible, not fitted from data. Note that they are defined day to day, not week to week like the persistence probabilities used illustratively in Chapter 1's closing lesson. A 0.97 daily self-transition probability compounds to roughly 0.97⁵ ≈ 85.9% over a 5-day trading week, and 0.88 compounds to roughly 0.88⁵ ≈ 52.8%, both broadly consistent with the weekly ranges used there.

The Markov property has a sharp, slightly counterintuitive consequence: because the process has no memory, the expected number of additional days remaining in the current state is always 1/(1-p), the same number as if the state had just begun, regardless of how many days you have already spent in it. A stressed regime that has already lasted 5 days is not 'due' to end. Its expected remaining duration is still about 8 trading days, exactly as it was on day one.

children.text: The Three Things an HMM Learns From Data

Every number in the table above, the means, the standard deviations, the self-transition probabilities, was chosen by hand for illustration. A real HMM estimates all of it from historical data. Formally, that means estimating three objects.

body.caption: The three parameters of a Hidden Markov Model

cells: The probability of starting in each state at the beginning of the series
The probability of moving from state i to state j each period; each row sums to 1, since from any state you must transition to exactly one state next, possibly the same one
The distribution of observed returns conditional on each hidden state

children.text: Lesson 2 goes deeper into how the transition matrix and emission distributions are actually structured and interpreted. Lesson 3 covers the Viterbi algorithm, which decodes the single most likely sequence of hidden states across an entire history once these parameters are known. Lesson 4 fits all of it on real Nifty data using Python's hmmlearn library. Lesson 5 addresses a question this lesson has deliberately dodged: how many hidden states should the model even have.

cards.definition: The unobserved regime the market is in at time t. Never directly labeled in the data, only inferred from observable signals like returns.
A table of probabilities giving the chance of moving from one state to another from one period to the next. Its diagonal entries are the self-transition, or persistence, probabilities.
The probability distribution of the observed data, such as a day's return, conditional on being in a given hidden state.
The assumption that the next hidden state depends only on the current state, not on the full history of past states.
A model that specifies, step by step, the random process assumed to have produced the observed data. An HMM's generative story alternates between choosing a state and drawing an observation from it.

body.title: Memorylessness in Practice
body.question: An HMM's stressed state has a daily self-transition probability of 0.88. The model has already been in the stressed state for 5 consecutive trading days. Using the Markov property, what is the expected number of additional trading days it will remain in the stressed state?
options: Less than 8.33 days, since it has already persisted a while and is 'due' to switch
Exactly 8.33 days, the same as if it had just entered the state, because the Markov property makes the process memoryless
More than 8.33 days, since regimes that have already lasted longer tend to be more stable
Cannot be determined without knowing the full transition matrix, including the other state's row
body.explanation: Because the Markov property makes the process memoryless, the expected remaining duration in a state never depends on how long you have already been in it. It is always 1 / (1 - p) = 1 / (1 - 0.88) ≈ 8.33 days, whether you just entered the state or have been in it for a week already. This is a direct mathematical consequence of the Markov assumption, and it is worth internalizing precisely because it feels counterintuitive.

body.title: A Structural Fact About Transition Matrices
body.textWithBlank: Each row of a transition matrix A must sum to ___, because from any given state the model must transition to exactly one state, possibly the same one, at the next step.
body.explanation: Each row of A is a probability distribution over 'what state comes next,' and every probability distribution's outcomes must sum to 1. This is a basic consistency check worth running on any transition matrix you estimate or hand-construct in the lessons ahead.

points: A Hidden Markov Model couples a hidden Markov chain over regimes with an observed emission process that depends on the current regime
The Markov property says tomorrow's state depends only on today's state; conditional independence says today's observation depends only on today's state, not the full history
An HMM is defined by three learned objects: an initial state distribution π, a transition matrix A, and emission distributions B, one per state
Each row of the transition matrix must sum to 1, since it describes a full probability distribution over the next state
Because of the Markov property, expected remaining duration in a state is always 1 / (1 - p), regardless of how long the state has already persisted, a direct and useful consequence of memorylessness
The next three lessons fit all of this on real data: transition and emission mechanics in Lesson 2, decoding with Viterbi in Lesson 3, and fitting with hmmlearn in Lesson 4
